messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 47
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Park Ranger
- Trauma Type: Child's life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 72

He is 47, married, and has spent most of his adult life working as a park ranger, a job he chose because he values quiet, routine, and the sense that the natural world makes demands he can understand. Before his son’s illness, he is the kind of man who rises early without complaint, packs his lunch the night before, and takes pride in knowing the trails by sound as much as by sight. He is steady, practical, and used to being the one other people rely on.

The trauma begins with what first seems like a minor illness in his child. His son becomes febrile and lethargic, then increasingly difficult to wake. The patient remembers the shift in his own body more than the sequence of medical details: the way his stomach drops, the way his hands shake while he drives, the way the emergency room seems to sharpen into bright, unforgiving edges. When he is told that his child’s condition is life-threatening, the words do not fully register at first. He hears them as if through water, while his mind keeps insisting that this cannot be happening to his family. He has spent years responding to other people’s emergencies in the park—sprains, dehydration, a broken wrist, a lost hiker—and he is unprepared for the helplessness of standing beside his own child’s bed and knowing that his experience, competence, and calm cannot protect him.

During those days in the hospital, he becomes acutely attuned to every machine alarm, every change in the color of his son’s skin, every shift in a nurse’s expression. He sits rigidly in the chair and watches the monitors as if vigilance alone might hold illness back. When the room is quiet, his mind begins to race through catastrophes. He imagines receiving a phone call from the hospital while he is at work, imagines his wife collapsing, imagines being told he was too late to do something, though he cannot say what that something is. He starts to replay small moments from before the admission, searching for the instant when he should have acted differently. He asks himself whether he missed a fever, whether he should have gone sooner, whether a better father would have noticed sooner. These thoughts do not settle; they loop.

His son survives, but survival does not restore the world to what it was. After the discharge, he expects relief to come in a clean wave. Instead, he feels left behind by the emergency, as if his body never got the message that the danger is over. He returns to work because he cannot bear the silence at home, yet even on familiar trails his attention keeps slipping back to the hospital. A radio crackle can make his chest tighten. The scent of disinfectant in a visitor’s restroom can pull him back so vividly that he has to grip a countertop until the feeling passes. He is startled by sirens, by sudden phone vibrations, by the sound of a child coughing in a parking lot. When he hears any of these, his first thought is always the same: it is happening again.

He becomes more watchful in ordinary life. He checks his son’s breathing at night, sometimes more than once, and does so in the dark so his wife will not see how often he is up. He sits on the edge of the bed listening, almost counting breaths, unable to trust his own memory of having just checked. He tries to conceal this from his family because he does not want to burden them, but the effort leaves him irritable and withdrawn. At work, he is still competent, but he is less present. He misses small details on the trail, forgets conversations with coworkers, and feels embarrassed when he has to ask someone to repeat instructions. The quiet that once soothed him now gives space for intrusive images: his son on a hospital bed, the beeping monitors, the fear in his wife’s face.

He does not like talking about the illness, partly because the memories come back too quickly and partly because he worries that speaking them aloud will make them heavier. He notices that he avoids family gatherings if someone’s child is sick or if there is talk of hospitals. He finds excuses to leave early. He also avoids medical television programs and cannot tolerate seeing IV poles, oxygen masks, or pediatric wards in advertisements. At times, he feels suddenly outside himself, as if he is watching his own life from a distance, moving through days out of obligation rather than feeling truly inside them.

What remains with him most strongly is not only fear, but a kind of mourning for the man he was before. He remembers believing that hard work and preparation could keep his family safe. Now he knows how quickly certainty can disappear. He still goes to work, still walks the trails, still returns home to his wife and son, but he carries the memory of that hospital room with him like a weight that does not set down.
